title: A second positive test
hook: With this test, one positive means about a 9% chance you are sick. What does a second do?

knows: counting people in a group to find a share
that a positive test for a rare condition is often a false alarm (base rates)
doesNotKnow: how a second independent result changes the chance
that each positive multiplies the sick-to-healthy ratio by the same factor

misconception: After one positive the chance is set, so a second positive adds little; or a second positive makes it near-certain (90% x 90% = 81%).
objective: The learner can explain that retesting the 98 positives leaves 16, of whom 8 are sick (50%), because each positive multiplies the sick-to-healthy ratio by about 10 (90% / 9%).
keyState: Second round reached: the twice-flagged group is 8 sick and 8 healthy.

claims.text: Of 1,000 people with a 1% condition, 10 are sick and 990 healthy; a test that flags 90% of the sick and 9% of the healthy flags 9 sick and 89 healthy people: 9 of 98, about 9%.
claims.source: Expected counts rounded to whole people: 10 x 0.9 = 9; 990 x 0.09 = 89.1 -> 89 (counts() in src/demos/probability/second-positive-test/model.ts). Exact Bayes: 0.009 / 0.0981 = 9.2%.

claims.text: Testing those 98 again flags 8 sick and 8 healthy people: 8 of 16, 50%.
claims.source: 9 x 0.9 = 8.1 -> 8; 89 x 0.09 = 8.01 -> 8. Exact: 0.01 x 0.9^2 / (0.01 x 0.9^2 + 0.99 x 0.09^2) = 0.0081 / 0.016119 = 50.25% (exactAfter(2)). The stage uses rounded expected counts, not a random sample.

claims.text: Each positive multiplies the sick-to-healthy ratio by about 10 (90% divided by 9%): 10 : 990, then 9 : 89, then 8 : 8.
claims.source: Likelihood ratio of a positive = sensitivity / false-positive rate = 0.9 / 0.09 = 10 (Bayes' rule in odds form). Rounding makes the stage's ratios approximate.

claims.text: This assumes the two tests err independently; a test fooled the same way twice by the same person helps less.
claims.source: The multiplication in c3 requires conditional independence of the two results given disease status; correlated errors (e.g. the same cross-reacting antibody) shrink the second test's likelihood ratio.

claims.text: The condition and the test are illustrative, not a named disease.
claims.source: Hypothetical numbers from the brief. Dot positions are a seeded shuffle (LAYOUT_SEED 9, layout only; counts do not depend on it).

recall.question: A test multiplies the sick-to-healthy ratio by 10 each time it is positive. Someone starts at 1 to 99 and tests positive twice, independently. Roughly what is their chance of being sick?
recall.why: 1 : 99 becomes about 10 : 99 (1 to 10) after one positive and about 100 : 99 (1 to 1) after two: roughly 50%.
